title: Monetary policy and the government's aims

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Trace the effects of monetary policy on the government macroeconomic aims - price stability, growth, employment, the balance of payments and the distribution of income - and weigh who gains and who loses.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: Which aims monetary policy moves
blocks.text: Monetary policy bears most directly on price stability, the aim of keeping the rise in the general price level low and steady. It touches the other aims indirectly. Lower interest rates tend to encourage borrowing, spending and output growth, which supports jobs; higher rates tend to cool them. The external position is touched too, since interest rates move exchange rates, developed in topic 6.3. So one instrument is asked to serve several aims at once, and the aims may pull in different directions.

blocks.heading: A rate rise against a 9% rise in prices
blocks.text: Suppose prices rise 9% a year and the central bank lifts its policy rate from 5% to 9%. Borrowing dearer -> households borrow less and save more -> spending slows -> firms raise prices more slowly, so pressure on the aim of price stability eases. The chain runs on: Marula Foods in Gobabis is likely to postpone a cold-room built on a loan, so output grows more slowly and jobs weaken, against the aims of growth and employment. Higher rates may also draw funds from abroad, tending to lift the currency and make exports harder to sell - developed in topic 6.3.

blocks.heading: One lever, several aims, different households
blocks.text: The same rise lands differently. Savers gain: a deposit of N$10 000 earning 8% instead of 4% brings N$800 a year instead of N$400. Borrowers lose: a N$20 000 loan costs N$1 800 a year at 9% where it cost N$1 000 at 5%. Households on fixed money incomes gain when the rise in prices slows. If Brazil's central bank lifts its rate sharply to slow a rise in prices, it accepts slower growth as the price of steadier prices - the trade-off every central bank weighs.

blocks.heading: Monetary policy and the balance of payments
blocks.text: Monetary policy reaches the balance of payments in three ways, and they can pull against one another. Through spending: a rise in interest rates slows borrowing and spending, and part of that spending is on imports, so imports tend to fall and a current account deficit tends to narrow - at the cost of slower growth and fewer jobs. Through flows of money: higher interest rates tend to attract savings from abroad, which can push the exchange rate up; a higher exchange rate makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, which tends to widen the current account deficit again. Through the exchange rate directly: a central bank that pushes its exchange rate down makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, which tends to narrow the deficit where demand for exports and imports is elastic enough to respond and supply can respond. Where foreign buyers barely change what they buy, or exporters cannot produce more, the current account may barely improve, while the dearer imports raise prices at home. For Namibia the second route matters most: to keep the one-for-one link with the rand, the Bank of Namibia tends to keep its policy rate close to South Africa's, because a much lower rate could lead savers to move funds to South Africa, draining the reserves that support the link.

blocks.heading: Monetary policy and the distribution of income
blocks.text: Monetary policy also moves income between households, although it is not designed for that aim. A rise in interest rates transfers income from borrowers to savers. Take invented figures: when rates rise from 5% to 8%, a household with N$40 000 in savings earns N$3 200 a year instead of N$2 000, while a household with a N$60 000 loan pays N$4 800 a year instead of N$3 000. Savers tend to be older and better-off households, while borrowers include younger families with home loans and low-income households buying on credit, so a rate rise can widen the gap between rich and poor. Where a rate rise cuts jobs, the low-paid tend to be hit first. Against that, a rate rise that holds inflation down protects households on low or fixed incomes, who spend most of what they have on food, fuel and rent and lose most when those prices climb. A rate cut works the other way, easing the burden on borrowers and cutting the income of savers. So the effect of monetary policy on the distribution of income depends on who borrows, who saves and how far inflation and jobs move - which is one reason governments pursue redistribution mainly through taxes and transfers, topic 4.3.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The aims monetary policy serves belong to the role of government in topic 4.1, the spending-and-taxation route to them belongs to topic 4.3, and the exchange-rate effects belong to topic 6.3.
